[batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] SES S.A. is a publicly traded, Luxembourg-headquartered satellite operator whose Pennsylvania facility, the Hawley Earth Station in Pike County, has one of the more documented ownership histories among the smaller facilities in this registry. The station was originally built by Comsat-General, a subsidiary of the Communications Satellite Corporation, as one of seven original US earth stations serving satellites leased by AT&T, and AT&T Long Lines subsequently operated it as a Satellite Operations Management Center functioning as mission control during satellite launches. On March 14, 1997, Loral Space & Communications acquired AT&Ts Skynet Satellite Services business, becoming Loral Skynet, and Hawley continued performing the same satellite tracking and control functions under its new owner. Secondary sources, including industry commentary and a crowd-sourced mapping entry, indicate the site later passed to RRSat and then into SESs MX1 media services division as part of the broader consolidation of the global satellite and media services industry, a pattern consistent with SESs known acquisition history, though this registry could not independently verify that later chain of ownership through a primary source during this research session and records it with correspondingly lower confidence than the well-documented AT&T through Loral Skynet history. The facilitys function, transmitting and receiving voice, data, video, and media signals to and from geosynchronous satellites, places it in a specialized category of communications infrastructure distinct from the general-purpose colocation and enterprise data centers that make up most of this registry. This research was carried out at the operator level in an earlier phase of this project.

reading.body:
The Hawley Earth Station in Pike County is a satellite earth station operated by SES, not a data center. It functions to transmit and receive voice, data, video, and media signals to and from geosynchronous satellites, placing it outside the category of general-purpose colocation and enterprise infrastructure that serves AI compute.

The facility has no published power specification in the data provided. Without a megawatt figure, its relevance to AI scaling cannot be assessed from grid or compute capacity. Pennsylvania has 14 mapped facilities across the state, of which only 4 publish power figures totaling 22.2 MW, and this campus does not contribute a number to that total.

This site does not matter to AI infrastructure decisions. Its specialized function in satellite operations distinguishes it fundamentally from the data centers, colocation campuses, and hyperscaler facilities whose power and cooling capacity constrain AI scaling.
